-RESEARCH NEWS— AND COMMENT-O Toward a Model of Academic Development: Schooling and the Acquisition of Knowledge PATRICIA A

ALEXANDER At times, it is hard to grasp the tremendous investment that Amer­ ican society has made in articulating and measuring the indicators, bench­ marks, or standards of knowledge ac­ quisition in the last 50 years
This in­ vestment has not simply been fiscal, although the money involved in certi­ fying educational attainment is truly staggering
Without doubt, the emo­ tional, educational, social, and political cost of this enterprise has been equally overwhelming
At the heart of this en­ deavor is a search for evidence as to what it means to be educated, a desire to document tangible, positive out­ comes from the orchestrated experi­ ence we call schooling
However, this very enterprise has become a wedge between educators and the public at large
It has also created tensions within the ranks of the educational community
The political and public fascination with such academic mark­ ers is difficult for many educators to comprehend or to justify (Feinberg, 1988)
These individuals perceive such efforts as detrimental to the very goals of education
But, others see this public outcry for documentation or substanti­ ation of learning as a critical opportu­ nity for reforming and reframing the educational experience (Hirsch, 1996)
Wherever one stands on this divisive issue, there is little solace in the current state of education, little sense that schooling is all that it can be for all of America's citizenry

Perhaps we should not be surprised that those in political and public arenas talk almost obsessively about stan­ dards, or turn to measures of account­ ability or competence, which seem to many in the research community to be unsoundly cast, as a way to document the effectiveness of learners, teachers, and schools (House, 1996; Wolf, 1998)
What benchmarks of "sound" academic development have we, as educational researchers, offered as alternatives

What more coherent and comprehen­ sive picture of learner growth and de­ velopment has been placed before the public as a reasonable counter to stan­ dards or measures considered imper­ fect or even counterproductive to the educative experience
If readers are expecting to find a de­ lineation of feasible alternatives to these standards or measures in the pages of this commentary, they will surely be disappointed
Any such delineation would be premature, in my judgment, since the educational community does not have the comprehensive models and theories of academic development needed to frame sound alternatives

That is to say, data regarding powerful instructional approaches or notions of best practice clearly exist in the ed­ ucational literature (e.g., Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1989; Cognition and Tech­ nology Group at Vanderbilt, 1996; Collins, Brown, & Newman, 1989)
Yet, these data offer only a glimpse of the long-term changes that students un­ dergo when engaged in formal learn­ ing
In fact, educators still have not embraced a concept of academic de­ velopment

Consequently, as a research community, we have not immersed ourselves in the kind of longitudinal, multidimensional, multimethod stud­ ies that would allow us to articulate credible models and theories of aca­ demic development
If you doubt this., look at the myriad of volumes related to teaching and learning

Do you find any discussion of the systematic changes that students should undergo cognitively, motiva- tionally, and socioculturally as they are becoming formally educated—not just for a year or two but across the life­ span
You will likely encounter indi­ vidual chapters devoted to cognitive, linguistic, motivational, social, and emotional development

Perhaps the idea is that if we understand these sep­ arate dimensions of human learning and development, we can make sense of the systematic changes that students experience as a consequence of formal schooling (i.e., academic development)

Thus, my intention here is to proffer the study of academic development as a viable agenda for the research com­ munity, one that can offer a worthwhile alternative to the more disjointed as­ sessment of knowledge acquisition characteristic of the American educa­ tional system

However, because many in the public and political sectors con­ tinue to equate schooling with the ac­ cumulation of knowledge, and because knowledge will likely remain a key component in models and theories of academic development, I want to focus briefly on the theme of schooling and knowledge
An Epistemological Orientation Certainly, questions about the associa­ tion between schooling and knowledge acquisition are not new to educational researchers
In 1979, when I began my doctoral studies, I was assigned a text that altered my thinking about learn­ ing and instruction in significant ways and that set me on a course of educa­ tional research
That book was School­ ing and the Acquisition of Knowledge by 28 EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER at GEORGIAN COURT UNIV on March 6, 2015 http://er.aera.net Downloaded from
The foundation for this work was an interdisciplinary gathering of psychol­ ogists, educators, and philosophers held on Shelter Island in San Diego in 1975

These noted scholars came to­ gether to ponder the complex relations between schooling and knowledge and to contemplate such perplexing ques­ tions as "How is knowledge acquired?" In the groundbreaking volume that arose from that conference, Richard Anderson, John Bransford, Ann Brown, Allan Collins, David Rumelhart and others sought to bring the concept of knowledge, as conceived through the eyes of cognitive psychologists, partic­ ularly information-processing theorists, into conjunction with schooling in the 1970s
Having just left the classroom to seek my fortune in the academy, I was captivated by these scholars7 reflections on knowledge and the acquisition of knowledge

In many ways, the theo­ ries, themes, and techniques captured in Schooling are symbolic of an era of knowledge research that remains un­ paralleled—an era in which researchers aggressively pursued questions about the structure, acquisition, retention, and influence of knowledge
It is hard to imagine that more than 20 years have come and gone since Schooling and the Acquisition of Knowl­ edge was published

So much has changed since ideas like schema theory entered our vernacular and dotted our educational landscape, even as other conditions and situations have contin­ ued in almost an educational time warp (Alexander & Knight, 1993; Alexander, Murphy, & Woods, 1996)

Since those days of information-processing theory, the educational community has been introduced to a plethora of new theo­ ries about learning and development that place knowledge in far more var­ ied light

We have become acquainted with such theoretical notions as con­ structivism, social constructivism, rad­ ical constructivism, deconstruction, postmodernism, critical theory, social learning, situated learning, cognitive apprenticeships, and situated cogni­ tion—to name but a few
As a result of this montage of new theories and their alternative percep­ tions of human learning and develop­ ment, knowledge has again become a focal point of debate
Aspects of this theoretical discourse center on the de­ gree to which knowledge is socially de­rived or individually formed, and on whether knowledge is internally held or externally triggered

I only wish to point out that, whatever one's epistemological leanings, there is now a deeper appreciation of the impact that society, culture, and context con­ tinually have on knowing and knowl­ edge (e.g., Greeno and the Middle School Mathematics Through Applica­ tions Project Group, 1998; Lave, 1988; Rogoff, 1990; Saxe, 1991) than in years- past

Many have come to heed the mes­ sages of those who speak of socially shared learning or the distributed na­ ture of knowledge (Resnick, Levine, & Teasley, 1991; Salomon, 1993)—some­ thing that would have seemed quite alien decades before

As a consequence of these debates, any ideas we may have had about the simplicity, unidi- mensionality, certainty, and constancy of knowledge in ages past—all those epistemological conceptions that Perry (1970, 1981) and others (Schommer, 1990, 1993) have documented in the young or unenlightened—have been supplanted with an understanding of knowledge as complex, multidimen­ sional, fallible, and dynamic

Even in the face of these new under­ standings and growing sophistication about knowing and knowledge within the educational community, the past research on schooling and knowledge has produced some powerful and replicated findings that should not be ignored
For one, above and beyond the shared understandings that arise from the sociocultural nature of human learning and development, there re­ mains an idiosyncratic quality to know­ ing and knowledge
Also, these person­ alized understandings can transcend any specific moment, place, or social milieu (Cobb, 1994)
Indeed, even the perception of knowledge offered here was not born out of any single social exchange or any one context
Rather, it stands as a legacy to the thousands of relevant encounters and experiences that have been woven into the tapestry of memory

Specifically, knowledge as portrayed here can be thought of as a conceptual scaffold, a foundation for subsequent learning that colors and filters one's school and nonschool experiences (Alexander & Murphy, 1998; Alexander, Schallert, & Hare, 1991)
So broadly de­ fined, knowledge signifies all that one knows or believes, without direct con­sideration of the source of that knowl­ edge, its explicitness, or its veracity
Thus, knowledge is not meant to con­ vey some canon of simple factual tidbits or litany of academic "truths" (Hirsch, 1996)
Rather, knowledge, from this epistemological vantage point, consti­ tutes the realm of human understand­ ings, whether accurate or incomplete, declarative or procedural, tacit or ex­ plicit
This is not to say that this episte­ mological stance represents consensus among educational researchers, or that questions regarding the source or au­ thenticity of knowledge are unimpor­ tant

To the contrary, multiple per­ spectives on knowledge have always existed in the educational research community and in the public at large, and will continue to do so (Reynolds, Sinatra, & Jetton, 1996)
These episte­ mological differences are nontrivial and help to explain diverse programs of and approaches to research and practice

Yet, the changes in perceptions of knowledge and the concomitant de­ crease in attention to internal process­ ing and individual understandings that have occurred since the 1970s cannot justify setting aside the decades of strong and replicable evidence that one's knowledge is a powerful and per­ vasive force in learning

• openness to persuasive arguments or convincing evidence (Murphy, 1999; Petty & Cacioppo, 1986); and, • judgments of relevance or impor­ tance (Jetton & Alexander, 1997; Stahl, Hare, Sinatra, & Gregory, 1991)

Not only is knowledge, in associa­ tion with other processes and out­ comes, of consequence, but the very quest for knowledge or understanding is also a valued goal, as well as a per­ sonally motivating and aesthetically enriching undertaking (Alexander, 1997; Csikszentmihalyi, 1990)
Many reading these words have dedicated much of their lives to the pursuit of knowledge and to the sharing of such knowledge in teaching and in writing
Thus, their respect for knowledge has a long and rich history—a heritage that is to be honored

While not failing to pay tribute to the everyday, informal, and incidental encounters that have unquestionably shaped our perspectives and con­ tributed dearly to our knowledge base (Alvermann, 1998), subsequent dis­ cussion focuses on the realm of formal or intentional learning (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1989)
Likewise, such for­ mal learning is considered in relation­ ship to the socially constructed and politically sanctioned organizations called schools
I want to revisit the mis­ sion of that San Diego conference of 1975—contemplating the relationship between schooling and knowledge

In so doing, I pose the following question: Has the last quarter century of theo­ retical and philosophical deliberations and educational inquiry endowed us with a new-found wisdom as to the nature of formal learning and the sys­ tematic, long-term effects such learn­ ing has on those who participate in that experience

In some ways, this question echoes the words of Robert Gagne in his epi­ logue to that historic conference: If we set aside, for the moment, our concerns with the questions of how people learn and look simply at the outcomes of schooling, what do we see

Or, in a more nearly ultimate sense, are they becoming more competent, more able to adjust to and cope with living in our com­ plex society, more capable of practi­cal problem solving, increasingly able to find a satisfying quality to their lives

My personal reaction to Gagne's in­ triguing questions is that we still know regrettably too little about the course of formal learning across the lifespan and about the anticipated changes that occur in those who set out on that course

Therefore, let me throw down the gauntlet to the research commu­ nity and call for greater systematic, multidisciplinary, and multidimen­ sional study of the formal educational experience and the changes, cognitive and noncognitive, that this experience evokes in its participants—what I refer to as academic development
It would be my sincere hope that this systematic, multidisciplinary, and multidimen­ sional research would result in new models of academic development that are both coherent and comprehensive
Aca­ demic development, as with other forms of development, refers to sys­ tematic change over time

In the case of academic development, the focus of that transformation is centered on the process of formal learning and on the outcomes that have been termed "schooled knowledge" or "scientific concepts" (Alexander, 1992; Gardner, 1991; Vygotsky, 1934/1986)
Of course, formal learning does not take place only in the classroom (Cole, 1996)
Yet, schools are institutions with an express educational mission (Dewey, 1916/ 1944), and one in which long-term par­ ticipation is mandated
For models of academic development to be coherent and comprehensive, they should pos­ sess certain characteristics, reflective of current wisdom on learning, develop­ ment, and instruction
First, they should represent changes that transpire in in­ dividuals over the lifespan of their for­ mal learning (Collins et al., 1989)

Con­ sequently, even though we may, as a society, concentrate resources on the schooling of our children and youth, formal learning for many—certainly for members of the educational re­ search community—continues through­ out one's lifetime
Models of academic development must, therefore, accom­ modate such continued growth and allow for an interface between formal learning prior to, during, and beyond the preK-12 school years

In a related sense, while contrasts between novices and experts in partic­ ular domains have been informative as to certain cognitive consequences of formal learning (e.g., Chi, Glaser, & Farr, 1988; Ericsson & Smith, 1991), such contrasts do not capture the grad­ ual and less dramatic transformations that are likewise central to academic development

Consequently, models of academic development must embrace all learners who undergo the educa­ tive process, including those who are neither truly novice nor clearly ex­ pert—in effect, the vast majority of in­ dividuals participating in this process (Alexander, 1997)

Moreover, from a methodological standpoint, a broad and deep understanding of academic development cannot be achieved solely through the cross-sectional investiga­ tions that have been the mainstay of experimental research (Kulikowich, Brown, & Bokoros, 1998)
Rather, sys­ temic, long-term, longitudinal investi­ gations must be undertaken at various points in the educative process, in­ cluding childhood, adolescence, and adulthood

Second, since the publication of Schooling and the Acquisition of Knowl­ edge, there has been a heightened aware­ ness that learning is not a "coldly" cognitive phenomenon, but encom­ passes motivational dimensions and is reflective of the social/cultural envi­ ronment (Brown, Bransford, Ferrara, & Campione, 1983; Pintrich & Schrauben, 1992)
This is precisely why the study of academic development cannot be re­ stricted to the study of cognition in iso­ lation from other developmental forces

In the work on domain learning in which my colleagues and I are engaged, we explore formal learning not only in terms of the relevant knowledge that individuals of varying levels of compe­ tence convey, but also in terms of the quantity and quality of their strategic processing, as well as the interests they manifest (e.g., Alexander, Jetton, & Kulikowich, 1995; Alexander & Mur­ phy, 1999; Alexander, Murphy, Woods, Duhon, & Parker, 1997)

Although I per­ sonally cannot fathom a viable model of academic development that does not attend to knowledge in some pivotal way, the possible configurations of cog­ nitive, motivational, and sociocultural 30 EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER at GEORGIAN COURT UNIV on March 6, 2015 http://er.aera.net Downloaded from
dimensions are extensive and allow for tremendous latitude and creativity for educational researchers (Ackerman, Kyllonen, & Roberts, 1999)

Third, I believe it is important to ex­ amine academic development in situ, as it unfolds during the interactions between teachers and students, as well as between students and students (Alvermann, Hichman, Moore, Phelps, & Waff, 1998; Cognition and Technol­ ogy Group at Vanderbilt, 1996)
Within this epistemological framework, learn­ ing is held to be both individual and so­ cial; that is, the learner and the commu­ nity are inherently related in formal learning

For this reason, it is essential to consider the social dynamic, even as we consider the variability within and across individuals as they progress from one learning environment or situation to another (American Psychological Association Presidential Task Force on Psychology in Education, 1993; Learner- Centered Principles Revision Work Group, 1995)
In effect, studies of group processes should not be cast as anti­ thetical to studies in which individuals are the unit of analysis, but rather as complementary pieces of a very com­ plex puzzle
Said another way, the days of building models of academic devel­ opment strictly from laboratory studies or highly contrived experiments are long past (Alexander, 1996)
This is not to disparage the contributions of such approaches, but to call for a model of collaborative, cross-discipline inquiry that values a range of research method­ ologies and paradigms
It is perhaps fair to ask why we should, as a community, aggressively invest in the study of academic development
Do we really need a sequel to Schooling and the Acquisition of Knowledge
Per­ sonally, I see the study of academic de­ velopment in terms of a moral impera­ tive
It is quite remarkable to consider that those who read this—despite vast differences in age, gender, ethnicity, or cultural background—share a common characteristic
Moreover, this formal educa­ tional experience was not brief, but en­ compassed years, if not decades, of their lives

In addition, even though some have elected to continue their formal education well beyond the period re­ quired, many in our society do not share a similar passion for academic learning and have had to be carried kicking and screaming into the educa­ tional experience

Given that schooling is such a com­ mon and requisite part of so many lives, it is startling to realize that we still understand so little about the sys­ tematic, long-term outcomes derived from participating in the formal educa­ tional process
We really cannot, in good conscience, ignore the ramifications of such a mandatory and pervasive experience in so many lives

For example, do we understand how the specific nature of mathematical instruction received by children in the primary grades not only impacts their conceptions of mathe­ matics, their problem solving abilities, interests in and attitude toward mathe­ matics at that juncture, but also how these outcomes impact subsequent de­ velopment

Further, what are the po­ tential consequences for continued aca­ demic development when students succeed at acquiring some body of his­ torical information but manifest no corresponding rise in interest in that domain or improvement in their ability to apply historical thinking in varied contexts
These are just a few of the questions that can be explored under the banner of academic development

Consider for a moment one startling fact: Despite the tremendous social- political investment that many soci­ eties have made in the schooling of their young; despite the rancor and de­ bate over the effectiveness or ineffec­ tiveness of our current educational in­ stitutions; despite the decades upon decades of research into learning and human development; despite the plethora of theories dealing with cog­ nitive, physical, social, emotional, or motivational development, we con­ tinue to operate as educational practi­ tioners and researchers with virtually no coherent and comprehensive model of academic development

Until we begin to articulate models of academic development that encompass hypothe­ sized patterns in learning outcomes, as related to schooling, and that allow for systemic inquiry and evaluation of for­ mal, intentional education, our under­ standing of the relationship between schooling and knowledge will remain undeniably constrained and regrettably fragmented (Perkins, 1992; Whitehead, 1929/1967)
Moreover, judgments about educational effectiveness may become relegated to more superficial and short- term ends (Donmoyer, 1998)

Perhaps one barrier to the aggressive pursuit of coherent and comprehensive models of academic development is the lack of consensus as to the under­ lying purposes of schooling (Berliner & Biddle, 1995)
Clearly, there are multi­ ple purposes for the creation and con­ tinued existence of schools (Dewey, 1916/1944)

Still, one significant pur­ pose of these social/cultural/political institutions we call "schools," particu­ larly in post-industrial societies, is to transmit critical understandings or knowledge to broad segments of the population (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1989; Phillips, 1995)
This is not to imply that the pursuit of knowledge is the sole aim of schools
Still, knowl­ edge remains an expected and valued outcome of formal education and a critical component in any model of academic development

In addition to the potential lack of con­ sensus on the purpose of schooling, we can probably intone a litany of expla­ nations as to why no models of aca­ demic development have yet taken root in this community Among the possible reasons are • the unbelievable complexity of learning and development; • the dynamic nature of human ex­ istence; and • the dramatic range of contextual and sociocultural variability
Even if we grant such powerful forces, they are the same ones with which we struggle in any of our efforts to research critical educational con­ structs
Certainly, in the past, when we, as a community, have determined that something matters deeply to us, we have shown astonishing ingenuity and persistence even in the face of formida­ ble obstacles

• synthesize the wealth of relevant theory and research that already exists, as a way to guide subse­ quent inquiry; • employ a range of quantitative and qualitative methodologies that can provide contrasting, but rich and complementary, pictures of aca­ demic development; and • dedicate the substantial financial and human resources to this en­ deavor that it deserves
Two additional epistemological/ ontological issues are of concern in overcoming barriers to academic de­ velopment
The first deals with the general pall that has fallen over the con­ struct of formal knowledge within the educational research community, espe­ cially in the last decade
As Sfard (1998) suggests, there are those for whom terms such as knowledge or concept no longer have a place in the educational vernacular

Even less extreme theoret­ ical stances on human learning have come to dwell on the tentativeness, boundedness, or completely individu­ alistic nature of knowledge (Greeno et al., 1998; von Glaserfeld, 1991)

Such stances may intentionally or uninten­ tionally call into question the passion­ ate pursuit of knowledge or cast a shadow over efforts to understand the systematic transformation in knowl­ edge resulting from formal education
Why dedicate oneself to seeking that which has so little permanence, gener- alizability, or certainty
If I were to categorize the last decade in the simplest of terms, I would stress its temporal or fleeting quality
This has been a decade seem­ ingly devoted to the "here and now/' where ideas can completely absorb us one minute, only to be considered to­ tally irrelevant and forgettable the next
It has also been the decade of process more than product, where doing seems to have become an end rather than a means (Sfard, 1998)
The human attention span has seemingly grown frighteningly short, even as our thirst for "seductive details" has become almost insatiable (Garner, Gillingham, & White, 1989)
It would appear that those theories of learning that emphasize process and, knowingly or unknowingly, disparage product feed into this moment-to-moment and situation-to-situation mentality
This leaves me to question what students, embarking on the formal educational journey, should come to expect for the time and effort they invest
What be­ yond the momentary stimulation, the grades, or the degrees should they ex­ pect to show for 12 or more years of education
Concluding Thoughts Even in delineating the potential barri­ ers to models of academic develop­ ment, I must reaffirm my perception that this understanding is worth what­ ever effort it requires

Even if we be­ lieve that our struggle to understand the developmental character of formal education will, at best, result in only a very limited and sketchy portrayal of an immensely complex and dy­ namic phenomenon, such a condition seems highly preferable to embarking on our educational journeys naively— equipped with only a vague hope that an intellectual promise land lies some­ where over the horizon

It is at times like these that I conjure the images of those intrepid (or foolhardy) voyagers in our ancient past who set out upon the waters of discovery with only crude mappings to guide their way—map­ pings that occasionally marked the un­ known with such daunting phrases as "beyond this point, there be dragons!" I recognize that this call for a concerted effort to chart the course of academic development may likewise be judged as foolhardy by some within this com­ munity But do we have a choice
Can we continue to send our children off on their journeys of formal learning with­ out a far richer and deeper under­ standing of what they should merit as a result
I would conjecture that we have man­ dated this educational right-of-passage for our children and youth for some reason and with certain expectations
Perhaps it is because we feel schooling is essential for these learners' ultimate survival, well being, or success in this post-industrial society, or for the very survival of the society itself
Maybe we, like Dewey (1913), believe that the formal educative process will give rise to a body of valued knowledge that will serve us throughout our lifetimes
Whatever our noble purposes, do we not owe it to our children and youth, and to ourselves, to chart this long- term venture and the systematic changes that it can or should evoke
Is it not time to recommit ourselves to the laudable goals of that Shelter Island conference of 1975 by seeking to under­stand how schooling relates to knowl­ edge and to knowing
